itineraries.title: Paraguay: Chaco Expedition, Mennonite Colonies & Untamed Wilderness
itineraries.subtitle: 11 days crossing the Paraguayan Gran Chaco from the capital to the Bolivian borderlands, through Mennonite history, Chaco War memory, and extraordinary wildlife.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May to September (austral winter), daytime temperatures 20-28°C, cool nights. Strictly avoid November-March: extreme heat (40-48°C), grueling roads, high health risk. The Chaco is one of South America's hottest regions.

map_keywords: Panteón Nacional de los Héroes Asunción

visits.text: Start at Plaza de Armas, Asunción's civic and historic heart, surrounded by its institutional landmarks: the Cabildo (now a cultural center), the Metropolitan Cathedral, and the National Congress. This square has been the stage for the country's major political moments since the city's founding on August 15, 1537 - hence the name Asunción, the feast of the Assumption. Take time to soak in the atmosphere, more relaxed than in many other South American capitals.

Just steps from the Plaza, the Panteón Nacional de los Héroes is unlike anything else in South America: construction began in 1863 on Francisco Solano López's orders, inspired by Paris's Panthéon and Les Invalides, but remained unfinished for 73 years - two devastating wars interrupted the works. It was finally inaugurated on October 12, 1936, after the Chaco War. Inside rest the remains of Marshal Solano López, President Carlos Antonio López, Marshal José Félix Estigarribia - hero of the Chaco whose path you'll follow for ten days - and the Niños Mártires of Acosta Ñu. Note that the Panteón's portico serves as kilometer zero for all Paraguayan national roads, including Ruta 9 that you'll take tomorrow. The changing of the guard takes place daily at 5 PM - a solemn spectacle worth witnessing.

Walk up to the Palacio de López - or Palacio de Gobierno - whose white facade stands out elegantly against the Bahía de Asunción in pure neoclassical style. Built from 1857 onwards on Carlos Antonio López's orders as a residence for his son Francisco Solano, materials came from all over Paraguay: stone from Emboscada quarries, bricks from Tacumbú, timber from Yaguarón, and ironwork cast at Ybycuí. Solano López never lived there: the War of the Triple Alliance broke out in 1865 before finishing touches were complete, and the Brazilian army occupied the palace for seven years, carrying off furniture and ornaments. Don't visit the interior (restricted government access), but walk around the esplanade on the río Paraguay side to admire the facade from the Costanera - when illuminated at night, it's breathtaking.

activities.text: Before leaving Asunción at dawn tomorrow, your arrival day is the perfect time to prepare for your Chaco expedition: stock up on water (plan at minimum 10 liters per person for isolated stretches), non-perishable food, medicines, and extra fuel (jerry cans holding 20 to 40 additional liters are recommended beyond Filadelfia). The supermarkets in Villa Morra neighborhood are well-stocked. Also check your vehicle's condition - spare tires, oil, air filter - because garages become scarce very quickly once you're on Ruta 9.

Late in the day, head down to Asunción's Costanera, the waterfront promenade along the Bahía on the río Paraguay. This is where Asuncenos gather to run, cycle, or simply watch the sun plunge behind the river's immensity - the Paraguay is so wide here you can barely make out the opposite shore. The sight of Palacio de López backlit is worth the trip alone. Take advantage of the moment to eat: waterfront restaurants serve surubí (giant Paraguay River catfish) grilled, a local specialty not to be missed before immersing yourself in the Mennonite cuisine of the coming days.

visits.text: Ruta 9, called the Trans-Chaco Highway, is one of South America's most singular roads: 835 km of asphalt stretching in a straight line from Asunción's outskirts to the Bolivian border. The first 50 km cross the Bajo Chaco (humid Chaco), an intensely green savanna dominated by caranday palm groves - the palms grow so dense and uniform they look like plantations. Watch the roadside at dawn: yacarés (caimans), capybaras, and dozens of aquatic bird species are common. After the town of Pozo Colorado (around km 270), the vegetation changes abruptly: palms disappear, replaced by the dry thorny forest of the Central Chaco - quebracho, palo santo, cacti. This is the invisible threshold between humid and dry Chaco, one of Paraguay's most striking landscape contrasts.

Make the most of roadside stops to observe the Chaco's characteristic fauna. Along Ruta 9, especially in early morning hours, you have good chances of spotting armadillos (several species), rheas (South American ostriches reaching 1.2 m tall), and all sorts of raptors perched on power poles. Around km 350, the landscape of dense dry forest with quebracho colorado and paddle cacti gives the Chaco its subtropical wild-west look - you'll understand why some travelers compare it to the Australian bush.

activities.text: Leave Asunción very early (ideally before 6 AM) for the 450 km to Filadelfia - count on 6 to 7 hours including stops. Ruta 9 is fully paved to Mariscal Estigarribia, but pavement condition deteriorates after rains and speed bumps are frequent in villages. Never take this road at night: wildlife constantly crosses and animal collisions are common. Fill up in Filadelfia as soon as you arrive - it's the last major gas station before the northern dirt tracks.

map_keywords: Museo de la Colonia Fernheim Filadelfia

visits.text: Filadelfia rises from the middle of the Chaco like an improbable Germanic mirage: ruler-straight streets, orderly houses, German-language signs, gleaming tractors in front of cooperatives. Founded on August 17, 1931, as the administrative center of the Fernheim Colony, it bears the Greek name meaning “brotherly love.” The 1,700 Mennonite refugees who arrived from the Soviet Union starting in 1930 - fleeing Stalinist collectivization - transformed in less than a century a thorny scrubland without potable water into a prosperous city of 18,000 inhabitants, capital of Boquerón department since 1993. Stroll along Avenida Hindenburg (named after the German president who facilitated emigration) and Avenida Trébol: you'll hear Plautdietsch (Low German) spoken as much as Spanish, and the local pastries in shop windows will remind you that you're not in the heart of traditional Paraguay.

The Museo de la Colonia Fernheim (also called Museo de Historia Mennonita), located on Menno Simons Hof on Avenida Hindenburg, traces the incredible odyssey of these settlers: departing Russia under Communist repression, they transited through Germany before completing their journey by ox-cart in one of the continent's most inhospitable regions. The exhibition starts with the 16th-century Anabaptist movement and arrives at the present day with photographs, maps, objects, and life stories. Allow 1.5 hours for a thorough visit - the panels in Spanish and German are well documented.

Just steps away, the Jakob Unger Museum is worth an hour's visit. Its name honors the first Mennonite settler to conduct systematic scientific studies on Chaco fauna, between 1950 and 1975. The museum divides into two buildings: the first presents the communal agricultural machinery from the colony's early days; the second houses an impressive collection of mounted animals - jaguar, giant armadillo, puma, anaconda - and an entire section devoted to the indigenous communities who inhabited the Chaco before the Mennonites' arrival. Don't miss the mural depicting the journey from Russia to Paraguay via several countries - it alone summarizes these settlers' epic.

activities.text: The Fernheim Cooperative runs practically everything in Filadelfia: the supermarket, the hotel, the hospital, the food-processing industries. Guided tours of its facilities - cheese dairy, slaughterhouse, sesame plant - are organized by the cooperative's tourist office (Avenida Hindenburg 131-S, corner of Avenida Trébol). These tours, in Spanish, German or English, give access to places normally closed to the public and help you understand the cooperative economic model: each Mennonite family holds a share in the cooperative and receives dividends, health insurance and pension coverage from it. Book in advance.

practical_info.booking: Advance reservation recommended at Fernheim tourism office

activities.text: Visit the market and cooperative stalls to taste local products: European-style aged cheeses (the Trébol brand is known throughout Paraguay), smoked sausages, sesame bread, and Chaco fruit preserves. It's also a good place to buy indigenous crafts from Nivaclé and Enlhet communities - mats, pottery, embroidery - whose pieces are sometimes sold directly by community members working in connection with the cooperative.

visits.text: Loma Plata lies 20 km southeast of Filadelfia: about twenty minutes' drive to enter a slightly different world. This is the administrative center of Menno Colony, the oldest and most conservative of the Chaco's three Mennonite colonies, founded in 1926 by 1,743 settlers from Manitoba, Canada - who were refusing the new English-language schooling requirement imposed in 1917. With 6,000 inhabitants, the town is smaller and more rural than Filadelfia, dominated by the Chortitzer Cooperative and its dairy processing plants (Trébol brand, Paraguay's major cheese brand). German is even more prevalent on the streets than in Filadelfia.

The Museo de la Fundación de la Colonia Menno, housed in the colony's former administrative building now converted, displays agricultural implements, ox-carts, and the first pioneers' tools. You'll learn among other things that 171 immigrants died waiting in transit camps for 18 months before reaching their lands, that the first problem to solve was water - the Chaco's water table being too saline for consumption - and that economic prosperity only really began in 1980 thanks to a World Bank loan that enabled investment in dairy processing. The adjoining tourism office (turismo@chortitzer.com.py) organizes tours of the Trébol factory and provides access to the lagoons at Laguna Capitán and Campo María.

Neuland, the third Mennonite colony of the Chaco, is reached from Filadelfia via a turn-off from Ruta 9 at km 413. Its name means “new land” in German - and with good reason: founded in 1947 by refugees fleeing the Soviet Union after the Second World War, it took in people whom other countries refused to accept, often widows, elderly people and families shattered by the war. A troubling fact: most of the first settlers were women, the men having been sentenced to Siberian labor camps by the Stalinist regime. The town of Neu-Halbstadt, its center, is the most modest of the three colonies but has a colonization museum and a monument to the Chaco War. Allow half a day from Filadelfia for the round trip and the visit.

activities.text: The route between Filadelfia, Loma Plata, and Neuland crosses typical Central Chaco landscape: thorny bush cut with estancias (large extensive cattle ranches), herds of gray-coated Brahman zebu cattle, and occasionally the silhouette of a century-old quebracho whose blood-red trunk gives the region its name (quebracho comes from "quebrar hacha," axe-breaker - the wood is so hard it was once exploited for railroad ties). Keep binoculars handy: rheas, armadillos, and sometimes Chaco foxes frequently cross the road.

In the Loma Plata area, several salt lagoons constitute excellent birding spots. The Chortitzer Cooperative's tourism office can guide you to the most accessible sites depending on season: bare-faced ibis, egrets, roseate spoonbills, jabiru storks, and Chilean flamingos regularly frequent the shores in dry season (May to September). Head out early morning - the light is better and birds more active.

map_keywords: Fortín Boquerón site historique Chaco Paraguay

visits.text: Fortín Boquerón is the Chaco's most moving site. Here, in August-September 1932, the first major battle of the Chaco War was fought - that deadly conflict that pitted Paraguay against Bolivia from 1932 to 1935 for sovereignty over a region both countries believed rich in oil (there was almost none). The Bolivians seized the fort on July 31, 1932, with 711 heavily equipped men; Paraguay's 1st Army Corps encircled them by September 9 and besieged them relentlessly for three weeks. The defenders surrendered on September 29, 1932: 320 Bolivian dead, 500 Paraguayans killed in the assault. This single battle officially claimed 3,738 casualties (killed, wounded, and missing) on both sides. The site today houses an imposing monument built from the original trenches and defenses. Look for the hollowed-out palo borracho (“drunken tree”) that served as a Bolivian sniper's nest - more than 70 years after combat, the tree is still alive.

The Museo de la Guerra del Chaco at Fortín Boquerón displays weapons captured from the enemy, uniforms of both armies, tactical maps and period photographs, some of them strikingly raw. What stands out is the imbalance between the belligerents: Bolivia had 3 million inhabitants against 1 million for Paraguay, and an army trained by the German general Hans von Kundt; yet the Paraguayans, better acclimatised to the terrain and remarkably led by General José Félix Estigarribia, eventually won the war and gained 75% of the disputed Chaco. Allow 45 minutes to 1 hour for a proper visit.

The military cemetery and memorials of Fortín Boquerón invite quiet reflection. The graves of Paraguayan and Bolivian soldiers lie side by side in respectful silence - a symbol of reconciliation in a war that killed between 80,000 and 100,000 people in total, nearly one combatant in four. Take time to read the epitaphs. Practical note: access is via a dirt track of about 26 km from the turn-off on Ruta 9 (Cruce Los Pioneros). The site can be reached in an ordinary car in the dry season, but a 4x4 is strongly recommended after rain.

activities.text: The round trip to Fortín Boquerón from Filadelfia takes a full half-day. Leave early in the morning to enjoy the relative coolness and avoid the afternoon heat, which can exceed 40°C in summer. The track crosses a dry forest of quebracho, candelabra cacti and thorny scrub typical of the central Chaco - an almost desert-like landscape that helps you understand the hell in which soldiers on both sides fought, without water, in scorching heat.

map_keywords: Aeropuerto Dr Luis María Argaña Mariscal Estigarribia

visits.text: Mariscal Estigarribia, about 75 km north-west of Filadelfia on the paved Ruta 9 (1 hour 15 minutes by road), is not a Mennonite colony: it is an ordinary Paraguayan town, or almost. Founded in 1944 on the site of the former Bolivian fort Fortín Camacho - retaken by Paraguay in 1933 during the Chaco War - it bears the name of the commander-in-chief of the Paraguayan armies during that conflict. General José Félix Estigarribia went on to become President of the Republic in 1939, before dying in a plane crash in 1940. The town, with around 1,500 inhabitants, is the last serious supply point before the north. Fill up with fuel without fail: beyond here, pumps become extremely rare.

The airport at Mariscal Estigarribia, Dr Luis María Argaña International Airport (IATA code: ESG), deserves a look from outside: its 3,500 m runway is the country's longest, built between 1977 and 1986 by Paraguayan military engineers with the idea of making it a commercial free zone. The infrastructure's enormity - oversized for the Paraguayan Air Force's small fleet - has long fueled theories about a supposed American military base, which both countries' governments have always denied. A curiosity in the middle of the Chaco.

activities.text: The Filadelfia-Mariscal Estigarribia leg is about 75 km, 1 hour 15 minutes by road on the paved Ruta 9. The road crosses the Chaco Boreal, an even more arid region than the Central Chaco: the dry forest of white quebracho and palo santo is more open here, dotted with thorny scrub and wide stretches of red earth. Drive slowly and keep your eyes open: Chacoan peccaries (tagua), rheas and many birds of prey frequent the roadsides. Parrots fly past by the dozen.

map_keywords: Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco Paraguay

visits.text: Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco is the largest national park in Paraguay: 780,000 hectares of xerophytic forest, created on 6 August 1975. Think of the size of Corsica - that is roughly it, and roughly as isolated. The vegetation is dominated by white quebracho, palo santo, samu'u and dozens of cactus species. The wildlife is exceptional: jaguars, pumas, tapirs, giant armadillos, giant anteaters, and the tagua (Chacoan peccary, Catagonus wagneri), a species considered extinct until its rediscovery in 1975. More than 460 animal species have been recorded in the park. Note: access requires authorization from MADES (Ministerio del Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible) - get in touch in Asunción before your trip.

At the heart of the park, Cerro León is a spectacular geological anomaly in the great Chaco plain: a Silurian sandstone and quartzite massif (444 to 419 million years old), 40 km across, rising to 604 m. In an almost entirely flat country, this isolated mountain is visible from afar and is a natural curiosity. For the Ayoreo, an indigenous people some of whom still live in voluntary isolation in this region, Cerro León is the centre of the world - a sacred place. The ascent is possible but only with a park ranger (contact through the Madrejón post, 220 km north of Filadelfia). The view from the summit takes in a 360-degree horizon of endless forest.

activities.text: Hiking or driving the tracks in the park requires a 4x4 and prior approval from MADES. The Madrejón ranger post is the entry point for the Cerro León area and the biological station; it is reached from Filadelfia, not from Mariscal Estigarribia, along about 200 km of dirt track via Teniente Montanía: allow a full day of travel and a night camping at the post. On the park tracks, set off very early in the morning (6-9 am) to maximise your chances of seeing wildlife - jaguars and pumas are extremely elusive but tracks on the ground are common. Giant anteaters, for their part, are more active early in the morning. Bring plenty of water - temperatures can exceed 42°C in summer (November-March) and drop below 0°C in winter (June-August), with night frosts.

practical_info.contact: Madrejón post, ~220 km from Filadelfia via Mariscal Estigarribia

map_keywords: Laguna Capitán réserve ornithologique Chaco Paraguay

visits.text: Near Loma Plata, Laguna Capitán is a private bird reserve in the transition zone between the dry Chaco and the humid Chaco. It is not on the road from Mariscal Estigarribia: plan a day round trip from Filadelfia. Listed as an “Important Bird Area” by BirdLife International, the site is one of the best birdwatching spots in Paraguay: roseate spoonbills, jabiru storks (the largest in South America, with a wingspan of 1.80 m), Chilean flamingos, bare-faced ibises and a wide variety of ducks migrate here according to the seasons. Hiking trails let you explore the edge vegetation between dry forest and flood-prone areas - an ecotone particularly rich in biodiversity.

The Central Chaco is also one of South America's most productive extensive cattle-raising regions. Along the return track, you'll cross several estancias with vast pastures of grasses imported from North America (buffelgrass, introduced in 1955, transformed the local economy). Herds of silver or coffee-colored Brahman and Nelore zebu cattle, supervised by gauchos on horseback, are a characteristic image of the deep Chaco. Also watch the ponds and water holes for yacarés (Paraguayan caimans) basking there during the day.

activities.text: The return leg from Mariscal Estigarribia to Filadelfia is about 75 km, 1 hour 15 minutes by road on the paved Ruta 9. As Laguna Capitán lies beyond Filadelfia, near Loma Plata, set off early to get there by mid-morning - the best time for birdwatching - then head back to Filadelfia before nightfall. Never drive at night in the Chaco: wildlife is everywhere on the tracks and the risk of collision is very high.

As you approach Filadelfia late afternoon, stop at the trackside to admire the sunset over the dry Chaco. The low late-day light gives the thorny forests and red plains an absolutely striking golden-orange hue - one of Paraguay's most beautiful natural spectacles, which you won't see again in town.

visits.text: The return to Asunción via Ruta 9 offers a chance to reread the landscapes in reverse. After days of dry Chaco, the gradual return to humid Chaco - which you perceive in the vegetation change around Pozo Colorado - feels almost liberating: caranday palm groves reappear, flooded areas and ponds reflect the sky, and dry heat gives way to gentler humidity. Around km 100 before Asunción, you'll make out the first structures of the periphery and, approaching the Remanso bridge over the río Paraguay, the capital's northern suburbs sprawling over the hills.

activities.text: The Filadelfia-Asunción leg is ~450 km, a full day of driving. Leave at dawn to reach the city before nightfall. If you have time, stop for lunch in the village of Pirahu or at a roadside bodega (snack restaurant) to try empanadas chaqueñas, filled with minced beef, olive and hard-boiled egg. A last practical tip: if you have enjoyed the Chaco, note that the Transchaco Rally, a legendary off-road race of more than 800 km on the tracks of the Chaco, takes place every year, in October in its most recent editions.

visits.text: The Manzana de la Rivera is Asunción's most endearing cultural site: a complex of nine restored colonial houses, facing the Palacio de López, that form a unique municipal cultural center. The oldest, Casa Viola, dates from 1750-1758 - its adobe walls and tile roof survived wars and demolitions. This is where you'll find the Museo Memoria de la Ciudad, inaugurated in 1996, which traces Asunción's history from its founding in 1537 with old maps, photographs, and models. In 1989, architecture students launched the “Save the Manzana” campaign to prevent its demolition and replacement with a parking lot - they won, and the city is grateful. Entrance is free; the café terrace on the second floor offers one of the best views of the Palacio de López.

If you have time before transferring to the airport, the Jardín Botánico in Asunción, north of downtown, makes a lovely 2 km² walk with some fifty species of indigenous Paraguayan trees, including specimens of quebracho and lapacho (the national tree with spectacular pink blooms). The Museo de Historia Natural y Antropológica, housed in Carlos Antonio López's former presidential residence within the garden grounds, displays collections of mounted Chaco animals - an unexpected transition between the nature you've just crossed and the return to the city.

activities.text: Use this final morning to buy souvenirs: Guaraní handicrafts (ñandutí embroidery, ceramics from the Guaraní ethnic group), Chaco leather goods (belts, wallets, artisan-tanned zebu leather bags), and Fernheim cooperative preserves if you haven't consumed everything on the road. The Mercado 4, Asunción's popular market, is the most authentic - you'll find everything from chimarrão mate to hammocks in caraguatá fiber. Allow an hour.

Transfer to Silvio Pettirossi International Airport (ASU), located about 15 km northeast of downtown Asunción. Count on 30 to 45 minutes outside rush hours, and up to 1.5 hours during peak traffic. The official taxi from downtown costs less than rideshare apps depending on timing - check with your hotel.

seo.h1_title: Paraguay: Chaco Expedition, Mennonite Colonies & Untamed Wilderness
seo.intro_paragraph: Ruta 9 draws a straight 835 km line from Asunción to the Bolivian border, crossing the Gran Chaco - 60% of Paraguay's territory but only 4% of its population. Over 11 days, this route takes you to the three Mennonite colonies founded between 1926 and 1947 by refugees from the USSR and Canada, to the battlefields of the Chaco War (1932-1935) and on to the 780,000 hectares of Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco, where jaguars and tapirs roam. An off-the-beaten-track itinerary that rewards independent and curious travelers.
seo.seo_hook: Paraguayan Gran Chaco: German-speaking Mennonite colonies, Chaco War trenches, jaguars of Parque Nacional Defensores, and end-of-the-world dirt roads.
featured_list: Asunción: the Panteón Nacional, kilometer zero of all Paraguay's roads, completed only in 1936 after 73 years of construction interrupted by two wars
Filadelfia: capital of the Chaco founded in 1931 by 1,700 Soviet Mennonite refugees, today a German-speaking city of 18,000 in the middle of the desert
Fortín Boquerón: site of the founding battle of the Chaco War (1932), with original trenches, military museum, and a still-living tree that served as a Bolivian sniper post
Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco: 780,000 ha of dry forest, Cerro León at 604 m and its jaguars
Neuland: third Mennonite colony, founded in 1947 by Soviet war widows whose husbands had been deported to Siberia by Stalin

places_taglines.PY::filadelfia: A German-speaking oasis born from Soviet exile in 1931
places_taglines.PY::mariscal-estigarribia: Last outpost before the infinite wilderness of the northern Chaco

highlights: Fortín Boquerón: first major battlefield of the Chaco War (1932), with original trenches and military museum documenting a conflict that claimed 80,000 to 100,000 lives
Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco: 780,000 ha created in 1975, with Cerro León rising to 604 m above sea level in the middle of the Chaco plain
Three Mennonite colonies founded between 1926 and 1947 by successive immigration waves (Canada, USSR, war refugees) who transformed a desert into a prosperous agricultural region
Exceptional Gran Chaco fauna: jaguar, tapir, giant anteater, Chaco peccary (Catagonus wagneri, rediscovered in 1975), rhea, and over 500 bird species

itineraries.title: Paraguay: Jesuit Missions, Red Earth and Río Paraguay
itineraries.subtitle: From UNESCO-listed Jesuit ruins to the banks of the Río Paraguay, taking in Guaraní crafts, Iguazú Falls, and the red earth landscapes of the heart of America.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May to August. Avoid December-February (oppressive heat of 35-40°C and high humidity).

map_keywords: Panteón Nacional de los Héroes Asunción

visits.text: Asunción's historic center can be explored on foot from Plaza de Armas, the colonial heart of the capital founded in 1537. On the square stands the Cabildo—the former seat of government restored as the Republic's cultural center—which is worth visiting as much for its architecture as for its permanent exhibitions on Paraguay's history. The Catedral Metropolitana, on the other side of the square, is one of South America's oldest cathedrals; take time to walk around the square rather than driving through it, as the atmosphere varies greatly depending on the time of day.

The Panteón Nacional de los Héroes is probably Paraguay's most symbolically significant building. Commissioned in October 1863 by President Francisco Solano López as an oratory dedicated to the Virgin and designed by Italian architect Alessandro Ravizza, it remained unfinished for over 70 years because of the War of the Triple Alliance—the most devastating war in South American history, which killed between 60 and 90 percent of Paraguay's male population. Only in 1936, after the Chaco War, did Colonel Rafael Franco have the building completed and declare it a national mausoleum. You'll see the tombs of Marshal Francisco Solano López, his father Carlos Antonio López, and Chaco War hero José Félix Estigarribia. Practical detail: the building also serves as kilometer zero for all Paraguayan national roads—eight major roads begin here.

The Palacio de López ranks among the most romantic buildings in colonial America. Francisco Solano López began its construction in 1857 on land inherited from his godfather, in neoclassical style tinged with Palladian influences, under the direction of English architect Alonso Taylor. Materials came from all over Paraguay: stone from Emboscada quarries, timber from Yaguarón, bricks from Tacumbú. In 1868, the Brazilian fleet bombarded it from the river and Allied forces ransacked it—European furniture, statues, and mirrors were carted off to Brazil. López never lived there. Admire it from the Costanera esplanade on the river side: the view of the illuminated Palacio at sunset, with the waters of the Paraguay below, is the best in the city.

activities.text: Climb up to the Loma San Jerónimo neighborhood for an entirely different image of Asunción. Perched on a hill above the river, this old working-class neighborhood is one of the city's oldest: its narrow lanes, ochre and turquoise houses, and stairways that open onto unexpected panoramas of the river make it one of the capital's best street art spots. Go in late afternoon—the golden light on the facades and the view of the Palacio de López below are worthy of any postcard.

visits.text: The Museo del Barro—officially Centro de Artes Visuales—is probably Paraguay's most unusual museum. Founded in 1979 by Carlos Colombino, Ticio Escobar, and Osvaldo Salerno during the Stroessner dictatorship, it brings together three collections under one roof: peasant folk art (over 4,000 pieces including Franciscan and Jesuit carvings from the 17th–18th centuries), indigenous art (over 2,500 objects from all the country's ethnic groups—ceramics, feather ornaments, Kamba Ra'anga masks), and contemporary Ibero-American art (around 3,000 works). What makes this place unique is its choice to present these three art forms on equal footing, without hierarchy. Allow at least an hour and a half to appreciate it—entry is free on Fridays and Saturdays.

The Jardín Botánico y Zoológico of Asunción occupies the former López family estate in the northern part of the city. While the zoo section isn't its strong suit, the historic López greenhouses—built in the late 19th century—and tree-lined avenues with century-old specimens make the visit worthwhile as a shaded rest between museums. The botanical section preserves a fine collection of Paraguayan palms and subtropical species.

The Manzana de la Rivera comprises seven restored 19th-century colonial houses aligned along El Paraguayo Independiente street facing the Palacio de López. Each house represents a different architectural period—from colonial dwelling to fin-de-siècle middle-class residence. Inside, the cultural center hosts temporary exhibitions on Paraguayan history and arts. It's one of the few cohesive groups of buildings remaining from the city's old colonial fabric: don't pass by without entering.

activities.text: In late afternoon, head to the Costanera de Asunción for a sunset stroll. This redeveloped riverfront runs along Bahía de Asunción for several kilometers: residents of Asunción gather here with their families, tereré and street food vendors set up from 5 PM onward, and the view of the illuminated Palacio de López from the river side is one of the city's finest. Arrive around 6 PM to settle in before the sky turns orange.

visits.text: Mercado Municipal N°4 is Asunción's most popular covered market and one of the best places to dive into everyday Paraguayan life. Vendors of manioc, chili peppers, fresh cheese, passion fruit, and chicha rub shoulders here from dawn onward. Arrive early in the morning to see the activity at its peak—after 10 AM the crowds disperse. It's also the cheapest place in town for breakfast: a hot chipá and a tereré to start the day right.
The Iglesia de la Encarnación, in the neighborhood of the same name, is one of the oldest parishes in the city.

activities.text: Avenida Palma is Asunción's historic pedestrian boulevard, lined with shopping arcades and craft boutiques. Here you'll find the best selections of ao po'i—the fine embroidered cloth characteristic of Paraguay—and ñandutí, the spiderweb lace of Guaraní craftsmanship. Prices are more negotiable than at the airport, especially if you seek out small family shops rather than stores catering to tourists.

End the day with a tasting of tereré and Paraguayan street food. Tereré is a cold infusion of yerba mate with medicinal herbs: it's both the national drink and a social ritual you'll see everywhere. Accompany it with sopa paraguaya—despite its name, it's a cake made with corn flour and cheese, not a soup—and beef empanadas. The many kiosks along the Costanera or in the center's plazas are the best places for this experience.

visits.text: Thirty kilometers from Asunción via Route 2, Itauguá is the world capital of ñandutí—Paraguayan spiderweb lace. The Guaraní word literally means “tela de araña,” spider web, and perfectly describes these discs of thread woven on wooden frames in radiating circles, imitating a web's geometry. The craft isn't of pure Guaraní origin: it derives from a Spanish lace from the Canary Islands, “soles de Tenerife,” introduced to Paraguay during colonization and transformed by women of mixed ancestry until it became something unique. In 2019, it was declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of the Nation. Enter the craftswomen's workshops—most downtown houses have their workshops open to the street—and watch the weavers work: a single piece can take several days depending on its size and the complexity of the patterns.

Atyrá, founded in 1580 under the name “aty-há” (gathering place) by the Franciscans Luis de Bolaños and Alonso de San Buenaventura, is one of the first Franciscan mission settlements in the Río de la Plata region. The flower-filled village in the Cordillera retains its 18th-century church and typical central square, with polychrome altarpieces and carved figures in the Hispano-Guaraní Baroque style. The atmosphere is more authentic than in Itauguá: fewer shops and more neighborhood life. Allow a day for the round trip from Asunción.

activities.text: The return to Asunción via the scenic Cordillera route—the "Guaraní hills" that stretch between Asunción and Caacupé—is one of the country's most beautiful drives. The red sandstone hills contrast with subtropical vegetation, estancias alternate with small white villages, and views regularly open onto the plain stretching to the Río Paraguay. Take the opportunity to stop at a local farm and buy artisanal cheese or caña paraguaya.

visits.text: Areguá is a small town on Lake Ypacaraí, with its historic center climbing a hillside beside the forest. Known as the Paraguayan capital of ceramics, it has dozens of workshops where artisans shape figurative pieces from the local red clay—from frogs to saints and figures from everyday rural life. The lookout at the top of the hill offers a lovely view of the lake below. If you have time, walk up from the main square: the route passes colonial houses, several dating from the 19th century. Allow a day for the round trip from San Bernardino.

Lake Ypacaraí, 40 km east of Asunción, covers 60 km² and has a maximum depth of barely 3 meters. It is famous throughout the country thanks to the song “Recuerdos de Ypacaraí”, composed in 1952, which celebrates its melancholy beauty. Its shores are lined with subtropical vegetation and fishing villages. Walk down to the water and watch the egrets and jacanas.

San Bernardino, on the eastern shore of Lake Ypacaraí, was founded in the late 19th century by German immigrants and quickly became the resort of Asunción's elite. The center preserves some traces of this Germanic architecture—half-timbered houses and gabled facades—mixed with modern constructions. The atmosphere is relaxed on weekdays, very lively on summer weekends. Stroll along the lakefront and watch the boats.

activities.text: Spend the afternoon on a lake excursion or relaxing on the shores of Ypacaraí. Operators offer boat or kayak outings from San Bernardino, allowing you to follow the wooded shore and spot waterbirds—cormorants, ibises, and herons are common. The light on the lake in late afternoon, when the water turns golden, is particularly beautiful.

visits.text: Caacupé—“behind the yerba grove” in Guaraní—is Paraguay's spiritual capital. The Basilica of Our Lady of Miracles, first inaugurated on December 8, 1765, and rebuilt in its current form starting in 1945, houses the Virgencita Azul, a 50 cm wooden statuette carved around 1600 by a Guaraní who had promised this offering if he survived a Mbayá ambush. Legend has it that the small statue was carried off by the flooding of Lake Ypacaraí in 1603, then miraculously found floating in a small chest—since then, it's been called “Virgen de los Milagros.” In July 2015, Pope Francis elevated the sanctuary to the rank of minor basilica. Every December 8, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims converge here on foot from all over Paraguay.

The church of San Buenaventura de Yaguarón is one of Paraguay's most overlooked treasures. Built between 1755 and 1772 under the direction of priest Carlos Penayo de Castro—construction finished just in time for him to be buried there—it presents a striking contrast: an austere exterior facade in white adobe with wooden columns that gives no hint of the baroque jewel hidden inside. The main altarpiece, standing 14 meters high by 6 meters wide and 3 meters deep, is the work of Portuguese carver José de Souza Cavados, who arrived from Porto via Buenos Aires and Luján: it dominates the choir in a swirl of gilding, polychromy, and baroque sculptures with French rococo influence, with the archangels Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael in their niches. Don't miss the polychrome wooden lectern or the carved confessional flanking the nave.

activities.text: The drive to Encarnación via RN1 crosses the agricultural heart of Paraguay: soybean and sugarcane fields stretch as far as the eye can see between red earth villages and estancias with long avenues of palms. Count on about 5.5 hours of driving from San Bernardino—plan to leave early to have time to stop at Caacupé and Yaguarón without arriving in Encarnación after dark.

map_keywords: Ruines jésuites Trinidad del Paraná Paraguay

visits.text: The ruins of Santísima Trinidad del Paraná are the largest and best preserved of Paraguay's Jesuit missions—and probably of those on the whole continent. Founded in June 1706 and designed by Jesuit architect Juan Bautista Prímoli, the mission housed up to 3,000 Guaraní people in 1728. The complex covers 8 hectares: a huge central square surrounded by the main church, the college, workshops, indigenous houses and a cemetery. Look for the pediment of musician angels in the church ruins—a row of stone bas-reliefs showing angels playing the clavichord, pipe organ, trumpets, Paraguayan harp and flute. It is the only known visual testimony to the missions' musical sophistication before the discovery of the Moxos scores in Bolivia. Listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1993 together with Jesús. Allow at least an hour and a half for your visit; the interpretation center in the former sacristy is worth a detour. Allow a day for the round trip from Encarnación.

Located 10 km north of Trinidad, the ruins of Jesús de Tavarangüe hold the finest architectural surprise among the Paraguayan missions. Founded in 1685 on the banks of the Río Monday, the church—designed by Spanish architect Antonio Forcada—was never completed: the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 brought work to an abrupt halt. This unfinished state is precisely what makes it unique: you can see walls open to the sky, trilobed Mudéjar arches (a Christian-Arab style, rare in the missions) and carved doorways with finely worked surrounds. Nowhere else in the Jesuit mission settlements of the Río de la Plata is this blend of Baroque and Mudéjar styles found. UNESCO-listed in 1993 together with Trinidad. Its name Tavarangüe means “the village that could have been” in Guaraní. Allow a day for the round trip from Encarnación.

activities.text: If you visit Trinidad at the end of the week, don't miss the sound and light show “Luces, Sonidos e Imágenes” offered on Friday and Saturday evenings starting at 7 PM (8 PM in summer). This projection mapping onto the ruins of the great church recreates the encounter between Jesuit and Guaraní civilizations, with projections of children, animals, and musicians that bring the ruins to life. It's an experience that perfectly complements the daytime visit and completely changes your perception of the site.

map_keywords: San Cosme y Damián mission jésuite Paraguay

visits.text: San Cosme y Damián is the smallest of the Paraguayan Jesuit missions, but it possesses a unique asset: the reconstructed astronomical observatory of Jesuit priest Buenaventura Suárez, the only one the missions ever built. Suárez, born in Santiago del Estero (Argentina) in 1679, spent 40 years in this mission settlement and made astronomical observations of remarkable precision, publishing his “Lunario de un siglo”—ephemerides for the 18th century—without access to any modern European instruments. The restored college today houses a museum on mission life and a planetarium. Allow half a day including the journey from Encarnación.

The Costanera of Encarnación runs along the Río Paraná for several kilometers and has become Paraguay's finest urban promenade since its renovation in the 2010s. Fine sandy beaches have been developed along the shore—a rare thing in Paraguayan cities—and bars and restaurants have multiplied. In summer, the place resembles a miniature Brazilian beach resort; in low season, the atmosphere is quieter but the sunset over the Paraná, with the lights of Posadas across the way (on the Argentine side), is spectacular.

activities.text: End the evening on the Costanera of Encarnación for the sunset over the Paraná. If you're there during the few weeks of Encarnación's carnival (usually January-February), prepare for one of Paraguay's liveliest celebrations: the "Carnaval Encarnaceno" is considered the country's largest carnival, with float parades, Brazilian dances, and a festive atmosphere that invades the entire riverfront.

map_keywords: Cataratas del Monday Presidente Franco Paraguay

visits.text: The Saltos del Monday are eastern Paraguay's great natural surprise. Just 10 km from Ciudad del Este, in the Presidente Franco district, three main falls plunge about 40 meters over black basalt rocks, creating a permanent mist that nourishes luxuriant vegetation. The Río Monday, a tributary of the Paraná, has an average flow of 100 m³ per second here. The 9-hectare municipal park is well developed: trails, viewpoints, and a 40-meter panoramic elevator inaugurated in 2015—the tallest in Mercosur—allow you to descend to the foot of the falls. If you've just seen Iguazú, don't underestimate this place: the solitude and proximity to the water are incomparable.

activities.text: The road from Encarnación to Ciudad del Este via Ruta 6 crosses the agricultural heart of Alto Paraná, one of the world's major soybean-growing regions. Thousands of hectares of soybean plantations stretch as far as the eye can see, alternating with groves of yerba mate and red hills. Allow 4 hours and 30 minutes of driving.

map_keywords: Parc national Iguazú Argentine circuit supérieur

visits.text: The Argentine side of Iguazú National Park can be explored in a day using two main circuits. Start with the upper circuit: a walkway follows the top of the falls, with views down onto the cascades plunging into the red gorges. Then the lower circuit takes you to the foot of the falls - be prepared to get soaked.

The Garganta del Diablo—“Devil's Throat”—is the climax of the visit on the Argentine side. A 1,100-meter walkway over the Río Iguazú brings you right to the edge of the system's largest drop: an 80-meter free fall spanning 150 meters, with a roar and mist that make the air unbreathable within ten meters. Go in late morning when the light shines from the opposite side.

activities.text: Border crossing Paraguay → Argentina: from Ciudad del Este, take the Friendship Bridge to Foz do Iguaçu in Brazil (the Brazilian side of the tri-border area), then the Tancredo Neves Bridge to Puerto Iguazú in Argentina. Allow for customs formalities on both sides—count on 30 to 60 minutes depending on how busy it is. Spend at least 5 to 6 hours in the Argentine park to see all the circuits.

visits.text: Iguaçu National Park on the Brazilian side offers a radically different perspective from the day before: from the opposite bank, you contemplate the complete amphitheater of the falls in a single panoramic view. The main walkway runs along the shore for 1.2 km and ends facing the Garganta del Diablo—from this side, you see it head-on and in profile simultaneously, from angles impossible from Argentina. The vegetation is more lush on the Brazilian side, and birds more easily observable: toucans, parrots, and giant kingfishers are common.

On your way back to Ciudad del Este, take a walk around Lago de la República in the city center. This artificial lake with its fountains and gardens is one of the few green spaces in this highly commercial city. The free-trade-zone atmosphere of Paraguay's second-largest city—a free-trade zone since 1961—is worth observing in its own right: tens of thousands of merchants and Brazilian and Argentine shopping tourists cross paths daily in a permanent bazaar.

activities.text: Border crossing Paraguay → Brazil via the Friendship Bridge. The Brazilian park can be visited in 3 to 4 hours; it's more compact than the Argentine side but the overall panorama it offers of the falls makes it an essential stop. Then return to Ciudad del Este to enjoy border life: the shops on Avenida San Blas and Curupayty street overflow with electronics, perfumes, and all kinds of goods at prices lower than in neighboring countries.

visits.text: Coronel Oviedo, halfway between Ciudad del Este and Concepción, is the crossroads city of central Paraguay—all national roads meet here. It's worth a stop for its cathedral and lively central plaza, and to observe the life of this commercial city in Paraguay's “heart,” without tourist artifice. It's also a good time for a typical lunch: look for a local market or a small eatery on the square to eat a bo'i chipa or homemade sopa paraguaya.

When you arrive in Concepción in the evening, head down to the port area for a first impression of the Río Paraguay. The river port of “Perla del Norte” (Pearl of the North) is one of the country's busiest: barges loaded with cattle and yerba mate dock here all day long, and at nightfall the river lights create a distinctive atmosphere. Walk along the Costanera for a few hundred meters—the upper town rises above the retaining wall, and the humid river air contrasts with the dry heat of the road.

activities.text: The long drive from Ciudad del Este to Concepción—approximately 493 km and 8 hours 40 minutes by road—crosses central Paraguay from one side to the other. It is one of the country's most revealing routes: Ruta 7 and then the secondary roads north take you through landscapes of estancias, zebu herds, red hills and sleepy villages where nothing seems to have changed for decades. Leave early in the morning to reach Concepción before nightfall and enjoy the sunset over the river.

visits.text: Concepción, “Perla del Norte” (Pearl of the North), was founded on May 25, 1773, by colonial governor Agustín Fernando de Pinedo under the name Villa Real de la Concepción—in homage to Charles III of Spain, a devotee of the Conception. Initially a military town for 40 years, it quickly became Paraguay's second commercial port, controlling the trade in yerba mate, timber, and cattle from the entire northern region. Its 25-block historic quarter preserves colonial mansions and 19th-century European-style middle-class residences, testifying to the prosperity of the Italian, Syrian-Lebanese, and Catalan immigrants who arrived in the late 19th century.

The Costanera of Concepción runs along the Río Paraguay on the left bank—25 meters high thanks to a retaining wall built to protect the city from flooding. The river port is one of the country's busiest for commercial river traffic: barges and lighters loaded with goods constantly move up and down the river to Asunción or the Brazilian Mato Grosso. It's one of the rare places in Paraguay where you still feel the economic presence of the great river.

The cathedral of Concepción and Calle Palma form the city's hub. The neoclassical cathedral dominates the main plaza, from which straight streets radiate in a layout inherited from the city's founding as a military settlement. Some beautiful colonial house facades remain in the adjacent streets—look for carved wooden gateways and interior courtyards.

activities.text: In late afternoon, go down to the banks of the Río Paraguay to watch the sunset from the port area. The immense river—nearly a kilometer wide at this point—takes on hues of gold and rust when the sun sets behind the Chaco on the opposite shore. Local fishermen return at this hour with their catches of dorados and surubís—the two most sought-after fish of the Río Paraguay.

map_keywords: San Pedro del Ycuamandiyú village Paraguay

visits.text: On the return road to Asunción, plan a stop in Tobatí in the Cordillera department. This Franciscan village founded in 1583 by Luis de Bolaños is one of the cradles of Guaraní-Franciscan culture: the colonial church preserves polychrome wood carvings and the central plaza with its historic well gives a fine idea of the urban planning of the mission settlements. It's also here that, according to legend, one of the two Virgin statues carved by the Guaraní Indian José originated—the big sister of the Virgencita de Caacupé.

Arriving in Asunción in the late afternoon, take a walk around the Recoleta neighborhood, which the itinerary has not yet covered. Its tree-lined avenues, art galleries and lively square make it one of the capital’s most pleasant neighborhoods for unwinding after the drive.

activities.text: The RN5/RN3 road from Concepción to Asunción crosses some of Paraguay’s most authentic rural landscapes: hills of the Cordillera sloping into valleys of red earth, estancias with wooden fences and zebu herds on pastures that are dry in the dry season. Allow approximately 6 hours 35 minutes by road for 398 km - leave early in the morning to arrive in Asunción in the afternoon and enjoy a final sunset on the Costanera.

map_keywords: Plaza de los Héroes Asunción market

visits.text: Cerro Lambaré is the hill overlooking the southern suburbs of Asunción on the river side. From the lookout at the summit, on clear days, you see on one side the urban panorama of Asunción spread out to the Palacio de López, and on the other the meanders of the Río Paraguay disappearing toward the Chaco. It's not a very developed tourist site—no cafés or shops—which makes it a good place for quiet sunrises and sunsets.

The Iglesia Santísima Trinidad in the Trinidad neighborhood, northeast of downtown Asunción, is a beautiful neighborhood church with a sober baroque facade and an interior decorated with 18th-century wood carvings. It's also the name of one of the capital's liveliest neighborhoods, where restaurants and bars cluster—a good base for dinner.

activities.text: The artisan market that sets up around Plaza de los Héroes—steps from the Panteón—is the best place for last-minute purchases: embroidered ao po'i, hand-tooled leather, palo santo wood sculptures. Prices are often more negotiable than in shops and the artisans present can explain their technique.

One last tereré on the Costanera—enjoy it the proper way by asking for a “guampa” (the horn or wooden container) and letting the street vendors prepare the medicinal herbs according to local traditions. Tereré is drunk by passing the guampa from neighbor to neighbor on the riverbank, watching the boats and egrets.

visits.text: Piribebuy—“fresh air” in Guaraní, because of its many streams—is one of Paraguay's most historically significant towns. Founded in 1636 by Captain General Martín Ledesma de Valderrama, it became the Republic's third provisional capital during the War of the Triple Alliance. On August 12, 1869, an allied army of 20,000 men besieged the town, defended by just 1,600 soldiers, women and children. Ordered to surrender, Commander Pedro Pablo Caballero replied: “I am here to fight and die if necessary, but not to surrender.” Paraguayan cannons were loaded with broken glass and stones for lack of ammunition. The church of Dulce Nombre de Jesús—consecrated in 1753—was the scene of the final resistance. The adjacent history museum displays weapons and objects found in the town's soil during construction work. Allow 30 minutes for the church and 30 minutes for the museum. Allow a day for the round trip from Asunción.

activities.text: After Piribebuy, head to the hills of the Cordillera around Paraguarí for a hike or a walk in the hills. Cerro Peró (660 m) has marked trails allowing you to reach the top in one to two hours from the villages at its foot. The views over the plains of Paraguay stretching toward the river and Argentina are among the country's most extensive. Local providers offer guides for more demanding hikes. Allow a day for the round trip from Asunción.

The return to Asunción via the scenic route of the southern Cordillera is a beautiful conclusion to this excursion. The last light of day on the red hills and villages of the interior creates one of the most memorable images of this rural Paraguay that conventional tours never show.

map_keywords: Cabildo El Centro Cultural República Asunción

visits.text: The Centro Cultural de la República El Cabildo, on Plaza de Armas, is the former seat of the colonial government. Its temporary exhibitions on Paraguayan political, cultural and artistic history offer a different perspective on the country - often more critical and less official than that of the national museums. Check the program in advance on social media.

Barrio Sajonia, in Asunción, is one of the city’s liveliest working-class neighborhoods, with murals and street art spreading across dozens of facades. Founded by German and Italian immigrants in the 19th century, the neighborhood retains some beautiful houses from that period alongside modern buildings.

activities.text: Last shopping session: if you haven't yet stocked up on crafts, Avenida Artigas and Mercado Central offer good selections of ao po'i, tooled leather, guatambú and palo santo wood sculptures. Avoid carandaí wood products which can pose customs problems in some countries.

Farewell evening at a restaurant with live Paraguayan music: the Paraguayan harp—the national instrument—and polca paraguaya (nothing to do with the Central European dance, it's a distinctive syncopated rhythm in 3/4 time) deserve to be heard in a good atmosphere. Downtown establishments offer harp and guitar concerts in the evening, especially on weekends—ask at your accommodation.

visits.text: Depending on your flight time, one last walk in the center or at the Jardín Botánico is in order. The Jardín Botánico is the quietest place in the city at dawn—hundreds of tropical birds wake up in the trees and parrots are visible from the earliest hours. If you're staying closer to the center, walk around Plaza de Armas again in the morning when it still belongs to the residents of Asunción and not to tourists.

activities.text: Transfer to Silvio Pettirossi International Airport, 15 km northeast of downtown Asunción. Count on 30 to 45 minutes from the center without traffic, 60 to 90 minutes during rush hour. Plan to arrive at least 2.5 to 3 hours before departure for international flights.

seo.h1_title: Paraguay: Jesuit Missions, Red Earth and Río Paraguay
seo.intro_paragraph: In 18 days, this circuit traverses Paraguay from end to end, from the colorful lanes of Asunción to the UNESCO-listed Jesuit ruins of Encarnación, via Iguazú Falls and the banks of the Río Paraguay at Concepción. It's one of the rare itineraries that shows Paraguay off the beaten path—living Guaraní craftsmanship, forgotten Franciscan missions, red earth landscapes, and the hospitality of one of South America's most overlooked nations.
seo.seo_hook: UNESCO Jesuit missions, ñandutí lace, Iguazú Falls, and the Río Paraguay in one of South America's most authentic countries.
featured_list: Asunción: Panteón Nacional built in 1863 and left unfinished for 70 years because of the War of the Triple Alliance
Yaguarón: 14-meter-high baroque altarpiece carved by a Portuguese master between 1755 and 1772
Trinidad del Paraná: Paraguay's largest Jesuit mission, founded in 1706 and UNESCO-listed in 1993
Iguazú: Garganta del Diablo accessible from the 1,100-meter walkway on the Argentine side
Concepción: “Perla del Norte” (Pearl of the North), founded in 1773, a river port on the Río Paraguay with a European historic quarter

places_taglines.PY::asuncion: Where 19th-century palaces meet the broad waters of the Río Paraguay
places_taglines.PY::san-bernardino: A German lakeside retreat where fin-de-siècle villas face tranquil Ypacaraí
places_taglines.PY::encarnacion: Gateway to UNESCO missions and Paraguay's wildest carnival, facing Argentina across the Paraná
places_taglines.PY::ciudad-del-este: Where three borders converge in a buzz of commerce beneath the thunder of Monday Falls
places_taglines.PY::concepcion: Colonial river port where Italian facades overlook the mighty Paraguay flowing north to the Chaco

highlights: Jesuit missions of Trinidad and Jesús UNESCO-listed in 1993—Paraguay's only two World Heritage sites
Itauguá ñandutí: spider-lace declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of the Nation in 2019
Cataratas del Monday: 40-meter drop with panoramic elevator since 2015, 10 km from Ciudad del Este
Battle of Piribebuy on August 12, 1869: 1,600 defenders against 20,000 Allied soldiers, one of the War of the Triple Alliance's most dramatic episodes

itineraries.title: Paraguay: Jesuit Missions, Waterfalls & Red Earth in 11 Days
itineraries.subtitle: From the colonial capital to UNESCO-listed Jesuit ruins, taking in Iguazú Falls along the way.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-May and August-October, temperatures 20-28°C, ideal for visiting missions and waterfalls. Avoid December-February (scorching heat 35-40°C, high humidity, frequent storms). Winter (June-July) is mild but daylight hours are shorter in subtropical areas.

map_keywords: Panteón Nacional de los Héroes Asunción

visits.text: Asunción's historic center unfolds around Plaza de Armas, surrounded by the Cabildo (now a cultural center and museum), the Metropolitan Cathedral, and the former National Congress building. Beneath this square, archaeologists have uncovered the foundations of the first colonial governors' houses—walk slowly and imagine that everything has played out here since the city was founded in 1537. The Cabildo houses the National Museum with collections tracing Paraguayan history; allow 45 to 60 minutes to explore it.

The Panteón Nacional de los Héroes is Asunción's most symbolic building. Francisco Solano López ordered its construction in 1863 as an oratory dedicated to the Virgin, but the War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870) halted work for more than seventy years—the building sat on its scaffolding while Paraguay recovered from a war that cost roughly 70% of its population. Inspired by the Panthéon in Paris, it was finally inaugurated on October 12, 1936, to house the remains of Marshal Francisco Solano López, unknown soldiers, and other national figures. The building marks kilometer zero for all of Paraguay's national highways. Admission is free—don't miss the flag-raising ceremony at 5:45 a.m. if you're an early riser.

The Palacio de López, the presidential residence overlooking the Río Paraguay, is worth walking around via the Costanera esplanade. Construction began in 1857 under the direction of English architect Alonso Taylor, commissioned by Francisco Solano López as a private residence—he never slept there: the war forced him to leave Asunción before its completion, and the Brazilian navy bombarded the building in 1868. Voted first among the seven treasures of Asunción's cultural heritage in 2009, it impresses with its Italianate neoclassical style, its columns, and its river-facing façade. Security restrictions prevent entry, but the view from the Costanera at day's end, with the building illuminated, is magnificent.

activities.text: The Loma San Jerónimo neighborhood has been Asunción's first official “tourist neighborhood” since 2013—and quite possibly its most photogenic. Perched on a hill from which Hieronymite monks once watched over the bay entrance during colonial times, this maze of colorful lanes, brightly painted houses, and murals feels like a blend of Cinque Terre and a Guaraní village. The 45-step mosaic staircase (Escalinata San Jerónimo), decorated by artist Claudia Godí, leads to the neighborhood's lookout point—the view over Asunción and the Río Paraguay is exceptional. Avoid weekday mid-afternoons: everything shuts down in the heat. In the evening, bars and restaurants come alive.

Asunción's Costanera, a long waterfront promenade along the Río Paraguay, is the perfect place to end the day. The setting sun tints the Palacio de López façade orange, joggers share the path with families pushing strollers, and a few chipa vendors (chipa is Guaraní cassava bread) offer their bread from trays. Allow 45 minutes for an easy stroll with views of the opposite riverbank.

map_keywords: Iglesia Virgen de la Candelaria Areguá

visits.text: The Museo del Barro—officially the Centro de Artes Visuales—is one of the most distinctive museums in Latin America. Founded in 1979 by Carlos Colombino, Ysanne Gayet, and Osvaldo Salerno during the Stroessner dictatorship, it established itself as both a cultural counterweight to the regime and an exhibition space. Its collection brings together more than 10,000 pieces across three museums in one: the Museo del Barro (mestizo folk art from the 17th century onward, ceramics from communities such as Itá and Tobatí), the Museo de Arte Indígena (some 2,500 items, including baskets, masks, feather ornaments, and pottery from Guaraní ethnic groups), and the Museo Paraguayo de Arte Contemporáneo (Paraguay's only permanent collection of contemporary painting, engraving, and sculpture). Admission is free on Friday and Saturday; on other days, expect to pay a few guaraníes. Allow at least two hours.

In Areguá, a town founded in 1538, 28 km from Asunción on the shores of Lake Ypacaraí, the historic center deserves an hour of wandering. Avenida del Lago, declared National Heritage in 1997, slopes down from the Church of the Virgen de la Candelaria (built in 1862, colonial baroque style) to the municipal beach on the lake—from the church's forecourt, the view over Lake Ypacaraí alone justifies the trip. Along the way, you'll pass old colonial houses with wide verandas that once belonged to Asunción families who spent summers by the lake. Since 2019, Areguá has been recognized as a UNESCO Creative City in the crafts and folk art category.

activities.text: The excursion to Areguá (a round trip from Asunción, about 31 km and a 35-minute drive on the outward journey) is also worthwhile for its pottery workshops. The pottery tradition is said to have begun with an artisan named Ricardo Pérez; today, dozens of workshops line the main avenue - you can step inside, watch potters work their black clay on the wheel and leave with a piece wrapped in newspaper. The Centro Artesanal de la Cuenca brings together the region's finest artisans. In August, the town holds the Feria de la Frutilla: since the 1920s, strawberries from the gardens of Compañía Estanzuela have spread throughout the region and become the local culinary specialty - enjoyed in pies, jam and liqueur by the lake.

visits.text: Make a stop in Yaguarón, 48 km south of Asunción, to visit the Franciscan church of San Buenaventura—one of the most beautiful on the continent and probably Paraguay's least-known jewel. Construction of this church began in 1755 and was completed in 1772 under the direction of Portuguese sculptor José de Souza Cavadas, assisted by Guaraní artisans trained at the Franciscan mission. The white adobe exterior displays simple Franciscan austerity. Push open the door and brace yourself for the shock: the 14-meter-high, 6-meter-wide altarpiece bursts with polychrome baroque sculptures carved from peterebi wood, covered in plant-derived gold and silver—the black comes from ñandypa, the red from urucú, the green from yryburetyma. Every figure tells an episode in the story of Christian redemption. The ensemble has been designated National Cultural Heritage and is a candidate for UNESCO inscription.

Paraguarí is a brief roadside stop on RN1: a quiet central square, kampala (dried meat) shops, and the rural atmosphere of the Paraguayan countryside. Nothing extraordinary to see, but it's a chance to feel the rhythm of rural life and buy cold tereré from a street vendor. Twenty minutes is enough.

activities.text: The RN1 highway from Asunción to Encarnación (about 370 km, 5.5 hours' drive) cuts through characteristic Paraguayan landscapes: brick-red earth, intensely green pastures, estancias with wooden fences, and soybean fields stretching to the horizon. Take the road early in the morning to see lapacho trees in bloom (September-October) or cotton fields in spring. Arrive in Encarnación—the "Pearl of the South"—in late afternoon for a first stroll along the Costanera beside the Río Paraná.

visits.text: The ruins of Santísima Trinidad del Paraná are the largest and best preserved of Paraguay's Jesuit missions—allow at least two and a half hours, plus a round trip during the day from Encarnación. Founded in 1706 by the Jesuit Juan Bautista Prímoli (a Milanese architect), the mission had 3,000 Guaraní inhabitants in 1728. Listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1993, it retains the layout of a true city-state: a main square, a large church whose planned nave with its dome would have reached three times its current height, a school, workshops, Indigenous houses and a cemetery. Look for the pediment of the musician angels—a carved frieze depicting clavichords, organs, trumpets and Paraguayan harps, the only known visual testimony of Jesuit music before the discovery of the scores at Moxos (Bolivia). The archaeological museum in the former sacristy houses Guaraní sculptures and a model of the mission at its peak.

Jesús de Tavarangüé, around ten kilometers from Trinidad, is the other mission listed by UNESCO in 1993 and the only one whose architecture features trefoil arches in the Mudéjar style - an Arab-Christian influence found nowhere else in the region's Jesuit missions. Allow for a round trip during the day from Encarnación. Founded in 1685, it was still under construction when the Jesuits were expelled from Spanish America in 1767: the church remained unfinished, allowing you to see the stone scaffolding as it was left abandoned. In the evening (Friday to Sunday, times vary by season), a 3D video-mapping show is projected onto the ruins - if you are there at the right time, it is a striking experience.

activities.text: The missions interpretation center in Trinidad, reached on a day trip from Encarnación, explains the political and religious context of the 30 Guaraní Jesuit missions that extended across present-day Paraguay, Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay between 1609 and 1768. The panels explain how the Jesuits protected the Guaraní from the encomienda system of slavery by creating self-sufficient societies with their own agriculture, music, printing and even astronomy. Allow 30 minutes.

map_keywords: Centro Astronómico Buenaventura Suárez San Cosme

visits.text: San Cosme y Damián is worth a day trip from Encarnación for two reasons. First, its former Jesuit college—the only surviving two-story building among all 30 Jesuit missions in South America, with its original ceiling paintings still visible. Second, and above all, its astronomical observatory: Father Buenaventura Suárez arrived at this mission in 1703 and, with the help of Guaraní artisans, built a telescope and a solar quadrant carved from quartz extracted from the basalt quarries of the Río Paraná. His observations, published in the “Lunario de un siglo” (more than 200 pages), amazed European universities with their accuracy. Today, the astronomical interpretation center inaugurated in 2010 bears his name and offers nighttime telescope sessions—book ahead if you are staying overnight locally.

Encarnación's Costanera stretches along the Río Paraná facing the Argentine city of Posadas. In summer (December–March), its developed urban beaches become one of Paraguay's most popular attractions. In any season, a walk at day's end is pleasant: the river is wide at this point, the sunsets are spectacular, and the city comes alive with snack vendors and families.

activities.text: Encarnación's downtown is easy to explore on foot. Stop by the municipal market to taste local specialties—vorí-vorí (corn dumpling soup), Paraguayan asado, and tereré (cold mate with yerba mate) are unmissable. The city was largely rebuilt after the reservoir behind the Yacyretá Dam was filled in the 1990s, flooding part of the old historic center.

map_keywords: Lago de la República Ciudad del Este
Puente de la Amistad Ciudad del Este

visits.text: The Cataratas del Monday are the Triple Frontier region's big surprise. These falls on the Río Monday—a tributary of the Paraná—reach 40 to 45 meters in height and 120 meters in width, split into three main cascades, and are framed by dense tropical vegetation. Since TripAdvisor confirmed their reputation in 2017 as Paraguay's most popular attraction, the park has developed substantial infrastructure: four lookout points, a 40-meter panoramic elevator (inaugurated in 2015, the tallest in Mercosur), forest trails, and a zip line. The Guaraní name “Monday” means “water that falls”. Allow 2 hours on site and bring a waterproof jacket: you'll come out wet.

Lago de la República, a small urban park in Ciudad del Este's center, is the calmest spot in an otherwise frenetic city. A 20-minute loop around the lake is enough to grasp the border town pulsing to the rhythm of international trade.

activities.text: Ruta 6 from Encarnación to Ciudad del Este (about 300 km, 4.5 hours) crosses the farmland of eastern Paraguay: soybean plantations to the horizon, glossy-leaved yerba mate groves, and a few estancias behind rusted gates. Ciudad del Este itself merits a brief evening exploration: it's one of Latin America's most important free-trade zones, a chaotic and fascinating border city where Paraguayans, Brazilians, Chinese, and Lebanese mingle.

visits.text: Iguazú National Park on the Argentine side (founded in 1934) is, by general consensus, the more immersive side of the falls. The Upper Circuit (1,750 m, flat) offers plunging views from atop the cascades: you look down, the water falls, and birds—toucans and swifts—wheel at eye level. Start here early in the morning for the light and the absence of crowds. Arrive at the park at opening—organized tour groups pour in from 9 a.m. onward.
The lower circuit (1,400 m) descends to the riverbank and brings you close to the waterfalls from below - you will come out soaked but happy. Do not forget a change of clothes.

The Garganta del Diablo circuit is currently closed: do not schedule this visit without confirmation that it has reopened. When accessible, a 1,100-meter walkway crosses the río Iguazú above calm water and reaches a viewing platform overlooking the main 80-meter-high waterfall. The water falls in a continuous white wall, the noise is deafening and the rising mist soaks everyone within seconds. When the circuit is open, the Tren Ecológico de la Selva (included in the ticket) takes visitors to Garganta station. The walkway had been completely rebuilt after the historic flood of October 2023 swept away 90% of its length.

activities.text: From Ciudad del Este, the road journey to Argentina is made by car or taxi through Brazil and then over the international Tancredo Neves bridge. Keep passports within reach for formalities at the Paraguay–Brazil and Brazil–Argentina borders, and avoid local Paraguayan, Brazilian and Argentine public holidays, when lines grow longer. A day at the park requires at least 5 to 6 hours on site.

map_keywords: Ponte da Amizade Ciudad del Este

visits.text: The Brazilian side of Iguaçu National Park offers a completely different angle from the previous day. From the visitor center, access is by park bus and then on foot: the panoramic walkway follows the base of the falls for around 1,200 meters, placing you opposite the amphitheater of 275 waterfalls arranged in an arc. While Argentina immerses you in the falls, Brazil gives you the overall panorama - this is the view that appears on all the postcards. Allow at least two and a half hours, including the walkway, viewpoints and, if available, the boat that approaches the foot of the Garganta do Diabo.

activities.text: Crossing the Paraguay-Brazil border via the Friendship Bridge (Puente de la Amistad) is the Triple Frontier's liveliest border experience. This 552-meter bridge over the Río Paraná connects Ciudad del Este to Foz do Iguaçu and supports one of South America's busiest road border crossings. Formalities can take anywhere from 30 minutes to several hours depending on the day—avoid weekends. Returning to Paraguay at day's end, soak in Ciudad del Este's atmosphere: shops open late, a bustling covered market, and gastronomy blending Paraguayan, Brazilian, and Asian cuisines.

visits.text: Coronel Oviedo, the strategic crossroads of eastern Paraguay's highways, merits a 20- to 30-minute stop to refuel and quickly visit the cathedral and central square. It's a lively agricultural town—market, motorcycles, mango vendors—and a window onto rural Paraguay, far from tourist circuits.

Caacupé, 54 km from Asunción, is Paraguay's spiritual capital and home to the Basilica of Our Lady of Miracles. Devotion to the Virgen de los Milagros—nicknamed “la Virgencita Azul”—dates back to a 17th-century legend: a Guaraní artisan reportedly hid behind a tree trunk to escape Mbayá warriors and promised to carve the Virgin from that same trunk if he survived. The wooden statue, about fifty centimeters tall, is preserved in the basilica; construction of the current building began in 1945, and it was consecrated in 2006. Every December 8, up to two million pilgrims converge on Caacupé on foot from across Paraguay. The basilica is open for visits year-round—30 to 40 minutes is enough.

activities.text: The drive from Ciudad del Este to Asunción (about 330 km, 5 hours) via Coronel Oviedo and Caacupé crosses the geographic heart of eastern Paraguay. Leave early in the morning to enjoy both stops without rushing and arrive in Asunción in late afternoon with energy to spare for a final stroll through the historic center.

visits.text: Manzana de la Rivera, directly across from the Palacio de López, is one of Asunción's few restored colonial complexes. It consists of nine houses from the 18th and 19th centuries—the oldest, Casa Viola, dates to 1750–1758—grouped around interior courtyards. Saved from demolition at the last moment in 1989 by architecture students, they now house the Museo Memoria de la Ciudad (an old colonial door, a map of Asunción drawn by Félix de Azara in 1787, ceramics, and archives), the Museo del Arpa, and several temporary exhibition halls. The terrace of the Casa Clari bar offers an unbeatable view of the Palacio de López—one of the capital's best photo spots. Free admission.

Cerro Lambaré, a few kilometers from downtown, is the hill from which you'll get the most complete panorama over Asunción and the course of the Río Paraguay. The site also has historical value: the Carios, a Guaraní people, had established a hamlet here before the Spanish conquistadors arrived in 1537. Allow 30 minutes for the climb and the views.

activities.text: For last-minute shopping, head to Mercado La Recova (handicrafts: ñandutí, the extraordinary spiderweb-like lace originating in Itauguá, ao po'i embroidered fabric, Paraguayan leather goods) or the shops along Avenida Mariscal López. Bagged yerba mate, tropical fruit liqueurs, and Guaraní wooden figurines make excellent souvenirs. After shopping, head to Silvio Pettirossi International Airport, about fifteen kilometers from downtown—allow 30 to 45 minutes depending on traffic.

seo.h1_title: Paraguay: Jesuit Missions, Waterfalls & Red Earth in 11 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: In 11 days, this tour crosses Paraguay from its capital, founded in 1537, to Iguazú Falls, taking time to explore the two UNESCO-listed Guaraní Jesuit missions—Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangüé—and a colonial astronomical observatory in South America. Red earth, villages of potters, Guaraní Baroque and tropical nature make for a journey away from the crowds in one of the continent's least-known and most authentic countries.
seo.seo_hook: UNESCO Jesuit missions, Iguazú Falls, an astronomical observatory and Asunción: authentic Paraguay in 11 days.
featured_list: Asunción: Panteón Nacional de los Héroes inaugurated in 1936, a replica of the Panthéon in Paris
Yaguarón: 14-meter-high baroque polychrome wooden altarpiece carved by Guaraní artisans in 1772
Santísima Trinidad: Paraguay's largest Jesuit mission, founded in 1706, UNESCO-listed
San Cosme y Damián: an astronomical observatory built in the forest in the 18th century
Iguazú/Iguaçu: 275 falls viewed from the Argentine and Brazilian sides, plus Cataratas del Monday on the Paraguayan side

places_taglines.PY::asuncion: Capital founded in 1537, called Mother of Cities, guardian of Guaraní baroque and the scars of the Triple Alliance War.
places_taglines.PY::encarnacion: Gateway to the UNESCO Jesuit missions on the Río Paraná, with urban beaches and a carnival renowned throughout Paraguay.
places_taglines.PY::ciudad-del-este: Border city at the triple junction of Paraguay, Argentina, and Brazil, starting point for Iguazú Falls from three sides.

highlights: Guaraní Jesuit missions: Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangüé inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993, preserving 18th-century sculptures and Mudéjar arches.
Iguazú Falls can be visited from Argentina and Brazil in two days, with the Cataratas del Monday (40 m high, 120 m wide) in Paraguay.
Yaguarón: Guaraní baroque altarpiece 14 meters high sculpted between 1755 and 1772 in peterebi wood, one of South America's most beautiful.
Caacupé: basilica of the Virgencita Azul, patron saint of Paraguay, welcoming up to two million pilgrims every December 8.
